solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Electrochemistry', electrochemical series and electrode potential

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: In the hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell, oxygen is oxidised at the anode.
Statement II: Catalysts such as finely divided platinum or palladium are incorporated into the electrodes of the hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.explanation: In this fuel cell hydrogen is oxidised at the anode and oxygen is reduced at the cathode: O₂(g) + 2H₂O(l) + 4e⁻ → 4OH⁻(aq). So Statement I is false. Finely divided Pt or Pd is incorporated into the porous carbon electrodes to increase the rate of the electrode reactions: Statement II is true.
steps: Pt/Pd catalysts in the electrodes (II true)
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Electrochemistry', fuel cells
solution.final_answer: Option D: Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: The molar conductivity of a 0.010 M solution of a weak monobasic acid HA is 40 S cm² mol⁻¹, and its limiting molar conductivity is 400 S cm² mol⁻¹. Its dissociation constant, K_a = cα²/(1 − α), is:

solution.concept: Degree of dissociation from molar conductivity
solution.explanation: For a weak electrolyte the degree of dissociation α = Λm/Λ°m. K_a then follows from Ostwald's expression.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ drops the (1 − α) term that the stem asks for. 1.11 × 10⁻³ uses α instead of α². 1.11 × 10⁻² leaves out the concentration c.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Electrochemistry', applications of Kohlrausch law: dissociation constant of weak electrolytes

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: A conductivity cell filled with KCl solution of conductivity 0.14 S m⁻¹ has a resistance of 150 Ω. The same cell filled with a 0.050 mol L⁻¹ solution of an electrolyte X has a resistance of 420 Ω. The molar conductivity of the solution of X is:

solution.explanation: The KCl solution calibrates the cell: G* = κR. The same cell constant gives the conductivity of X, and Λm = κ/c with c in mol m⁻³ for SI units.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1.0 S m² mol⁻¹ divides by c in mol L⁻¹ without converting to mol m⁻³. 7.84 × 10⁻³ multiplies by the resistance ratio the wrong way round. 5.0 × 10⁻² is the conductivity, not the molar conductivity.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Electrochemistry', measurement of the conductivity of ionic solutions

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (electrode reaction) with List-II (where it takes place).

List-I:
A. Pb(s) + SO₄²⁻(aq) → PbSO₄(s) + 2e⁻
B. PbO₂(s) + SO₄²⁻(aq) + 4H⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ → PbSO₄(s) + 2H₂O(l)
C. Zn(s) → Zn²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻
D. MnO₂ + NH₄⁺ + e⁻ → MnO(OH) + NH₃

List-II:
I. Cathode of the dry cell
II. Anode of the lead storage battery during discharge
III. Anode of the dry cell
IV. Cathode of the lead storage battery during discharge

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Electrode reactions of the lead storage battery and the dry cell
solution.explanation: Oxidation (loss of electrons) occurs at the anode and reduction at the cathode. During discharge of the lead storage battery, lead is oxidised to PbSO₄ and PbO₂ is reduced to PbSO₄. In the dry cell, the zinc container is oxidised and MnO₂ is reduced (Mn: +4 → +3).
steps: Pb → PbSO₄ (oxidation) → lead battery anode → II
PbO₂ → PbSO₄ (reduction) → lead battery cathode → IV
Zn → Zn²⁺ (oxidation) → dry cell anode → III
MnO₂ → MnO(OH) (reduction) → dry cell cathode → I
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes swap anode and cathode in one of the two cells, or put the zinc oxidation in the lead battery.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Electrochemistry', batteries: dry cell and lead storage battery
solution.final_answer: Option C: A-II, B-IV, C-III, D-I

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): At the same concentration and temperature, an aqueous solution of HCl conducts electricity better than an aqueous solution of NaCl.
Reason (R): Pure hydrogen chloride is a gas at room temperature, whereas pure sodium chloride is a solid.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Ionic conductivities of H⁺ and Na⁺
solution.explanation: Both HCl and NaCl are strong electrolytes, so the difference lies in the ions. The limiting molar conductivity of H⁺ (about 350 S cm² mol⁻¹) is about seven times that of Na⁺ (about 50 S cm² mol⁻¹), so the HCl solution conducts better: A is true. R is also true, but the physical state of the pure substances has nothing to do with the conductance of their aqueous solutions, so R does not explain A.
steps: Λ°(H⁺) ≈ 350 vs Λ°(Na⁺) ≈ 50 S cm² mol⁻¹ → HCl(aq) conducts better (A true)
HCl is a gas and NaCl a solid (R true) but irrelevant to conduction in solution
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Electrochemistry', Kohlrausch law: limiting molar conductivities of ions
solution.final_answer: Option B: Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: For a first-order reaction, the percentage of the initial reactant that remains unreacted after three half-lives is:

solution.concept: Successive half-lives of a first-order reaction
solution.explanation: The half-life of a first-order reaction does not depend on concentration, so the amount halves in every half-life.
solution.why_others_wrong: 25% is after two half-lives. 33.3% divides 100% by three. 87.5% is the percentage that has reacted.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Chemical Kinetics', half-life of a reaction

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: The instantaneous rate of the reaction R → P at time t is obtained from the plot of [R] against time as:

options.text: The slope of the straight line joining the starting point and the point at time t
The negative of the slope of the tangent to the curve at time t
The area under the curve up to time t
The intercept of the curve on the concentration axis

solution.explanation: The instantaneous rate is −d[R]/dt, the limit of the average rate as the time interval tends to zero. Graphically it is found by drawing a tangent to the [R]–t curve at time t and taking the negative of its slope.
steps: Draw a tangent at t; rate = −(slope of tangent)
solution.why_others_wrong: The line joining two points gives an average rate. The area under the curve and the intercept have no such meaning.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Chemical Kinetics', rate of a chemical reaction: instantaneous rate
solution.final_answer: Option B: The negative of the slope of the tangent to the curve at time t

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: For two reactions with the same pre-exponential factor at the same temperature, the reaction with the higher activation energy has the smaller rate constant.
Statement II: The rate constant of a first-order reaction has the unit mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Arrhenius equation and units of k
solution.explanation: k = A e^(−Ea/RT): with A and T fixed, a larger Ea gives a smaller e^(−Ea/RT) and so a smaller k. Statement I is true. For a first-order reaction k = rate/[R] has the unit s⁻¹; mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹ is the unit for a zero-order reaction. Statement II is false.
steps: k = A e^(−Ea/RT): larger Ea → smaller k (I true)
First order: unit of k is s⁻¹ (II false)
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Chemical Kinetics', temperature dependence of the rate of a reaction; units of rate constant
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: A reaction has an activation energy of 28.7 kJ mol⁻¹. At 300 K, the fraction of molecules having energy equal to or greater than the activation energy, e^(−Ea/RT), is (2.303RT = 5.74 kJ mol⁻¹ at 300 K):

solution.concept: Fraction of effective molecules in the Arrhenius equation
solution.explanation: In k = A e^(−Ea/RT), the factor e^(−Ea/RT) is the fraction of molecules with energy at least Ea. Taking logarithms to base 10: log f = −Ea/(2.303RT).
solution.why_others_wrong: 6.7 × 10⁻³ is e⁻⁵: it uses 2.303RT in place of RT inside the natural exponential. 1 × 10⁵ drops the minus sign (a fraction cannot exceed 1). 2 × 10⁻¹ is simply 5.74/28.7.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Chemical Kinetics', temperature dependence of the rate of a reaction

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: The rate constant of a reaction nearly doubles for every 10 K rise in temperature. If this holds, by what factor does the rate constant increase when the temperature is raised from 300 K to 330 K?

solution.concept: Effect of temperature on rate constant
solution.explanation: Each 10 K rise multiplies k by about 2. A 30 K rise contains three such steps, so the factors multiply.
solution.why_others_wrong: 6 adds the factors (2 + 2 + 2) instead of multiplying them. 3 counts the steps. 9 is 3².
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Chemical Kinetics', temperature dependence of the rate of a reaction

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The thermal decomposition of HI on a gold surface is a zero-order reaction.
Reason (R): Gold is a noble metal that does not corrode in air.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.explanation: NCERT gives the decomposition of HI on a gold surface as an example of a zero-order reaction, so A is true. Gold is indeed unreactive towards air, so R is true. But R does not explain A: the zero order arises because the gold surface is saturated with HI molecules, so the rate does not depend on the gas concentration.
steps: Reason for zero order: saturated catalyst surface, not resistance to corrosion
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Chemical Kinetics', zero order reactions
solution.final_answer: Option B: Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (expression) with List-II (what it represents).

List-I:
A. k = (2.303/t) log([R]₀/[R])
B. [R] = [R]₀ − kt
C. t½ = 0.693/k
D. t½ = [R]₀/2k

List-II:
I. Integrated rate equation of a zero-order reaction
II. Half-life of a first-order reaction
III. Integrated rate equation of a first-order reaction
IV. Half-life of a zero-order reaction

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: For zero order, [R] falls linearly with time and t½ = [R]₀/2k. For first order, k = (2.303/t) log([R]₀/[R]) and t½ = 0.693/k.
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes interchange the zero- and first-order equations or their half-lives.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Chemical Kinetics', integrated rate equations
solution.final_answer: Option D: A-III, B-I, C-II, D-IV

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Two first-order reactions, A → products (t½ = 10 min) and B → products (t½ = 20 min), are started at the same time with equal initial concentrations of A and B. After 40 min, the ratio [A] : [B] is:

solution.explanation: In 40 min A goes through 40/10 = 4 half-lives and B through 40/20 = 2 half-lives.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1 : 2 is just the ratio of the half-lives. 4 : 1 inverts the ratio. 1 : 16 is the fraction of A left, not the ratio of A to B.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Chemical Kinetics', half-life of a reaction

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about a catalyst are correct?

(a) A catalyst is consumed permanently in the reaction it catalyses.
(b) A catalyst does not change the equilibrium constant of a reversible reaction.
(c) A catalyst increases the rate of the forward reaction only.
(d) A catalyst lowers the activation energy of the forward and the backward reactions by the same amount.
(e) A small amount of a catalyst can catalyse a large amount of reactants.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: A catalyst provides an alternative pathway of lower activation energy and is regenerated at the end of the reaction. The energy barrier falls equally for both directions, so both rates rise by the same factor and the position of equilibrium (K) is unchanged. A small amount of catalyst is enough for a large amount of reactants.
steps: (c) False: both directions are speeded up
solution.why_others_wrong: Options containing (a) or (c) are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Chemical Kinetics', effect of catalyst

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: For a first-order reaction, a plot of log[R] (common logarithm) against time t is a straight line whose slope is:

solution.concept: Graphical form of the first-order rate equation
solution.explanation: The integrated first-order equation ln[R] = ln[R]₀ − kt becomes, in common logarithms, log[R] = log[R]₀ − kt/2.303.
solution.why_others_wrong: −k is the slope of the ln[R] plot, not the log[R] plot. −2.303k multiplies instead of dividing. The slope is negative because [R] falls with time.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Chemical Kinetics', first order reactions

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.question_text: The Cl–Cl bond distance in the chlorine molecule is 198 pm. The covalent (atomic) radius of chlorine is:

solution.explanation: For a non-metal forming a homonuclear diatomic molecule, the covalent radius is half the distance between the nuclei of the two bonded atoms.
steps: Covalent radius = ½ × internuclear distance = 198 / 2 = 99 pm
solution.why_others_wrong: 198 pm is the whole bond length. 396 pm doubles it, and 49.5 pm halves the radius again.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties', atomic radius

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.question_text: An element has the ground-state electronic configuration [Ne] 3s² 3p³. Its position in the periodic table is:

solution.concept: Locating an element from its configuration
solution.explanation: The period is the principal quantum number of the valence shell. For a p-block element, the group number is 10 + (number of s and p valence electrons).
solution.why_others_wrong: Group 13 counts only the s electrons plus one p electron. Period 2 ignores the [Ne] core. Group 5 is a d-block group; the old 'VA' label is now group 15.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties', electronic configurations and types of elements: p-block

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: The s-block and p-block elements together are called the representative or main group elements.
Statement II: The f-block elements are called the inner-transition elements.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Types of elements in the periodic table
solution.explanation: Both statements are the standard classification: s- and p-block elements are the representative (main group) elements, d-block elements are the transition elements, and the lanthanoids and actinoids (f-block) are the inner-transition elements.
steps: s + p blocks → representative elements (I true)
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties', electronic configurations and types of elements
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.question_text: Which of the following pairs of elements shows a diagonal relationship?

solution.explanation: The first member of groups 1 and 2 (Li, Be) resembles the second member of the next group (Mg, Al) more than its own group. This similarity between diagonally placed elements is called a diagonal relationship.
solution.why_others_wrong: Be–Mg, Li–Na and B–Al are pairs in the same group, not diagonal pairs.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties', anomalous properties of second period elements

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): Among the elements of the second period, neon has the lowest first ionisation enthalpy.
Reason (R): Neon has a completely filled valence shell, 2s² 2p⁶.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.explanation: A completely filled valence shell is very stable, and neon also has the highest effective nuclear charge in the period. Its first ionisation enthalpy is therefore the highest, not the lowest, in period 2 (lithium has the lowest). A is false; R is true.
steps: Closed shell + high Z_eff → highest ΔiH₁ in period 2 (A false)
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties', ionisation enthalpy
solution.final_answer: Option D: A is false but R is true.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (general outer electronic configuration) with List-II (group).

List-I:
A. [noble gas] ns² np⁶
B. [noble gas] (n−1)d¹⁰ ns²
C. [noble gas] ns¹
D. [noble gas] (n−1)d⁵ ns¹

List-II:
I. Group 6
II. Group 1
III. Group 18
IV. Group 12

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Group from the outer electronic configuration
solution.explanation: For s-block elements the group equals the number of s electrons; for p-block, 10 + (s + p electrons); for d-block, the number of (n−1)d + ns electrons.
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes swap group 1 with group 6, or group 18 with group 12.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties', electronic configurations and types of elements
solution.final_answer: Option C: A-III, B-IV, C-II, D-I

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.question_text:
Which of the following general formulae (M = metal, E = element of the group) are correct?

(a) Oxide of a group 2 element: MO
(b) Simple hydride of a group 14 element: EH₄
(c) Simple hydride of a group 16 element: EH₃
(d) Simple hydride of a group 15 element: EH₂
(e) Oxide of a group 13 element in its group oxidation state: E₂O₃

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: The usual valence of a representative element equals the number of valence electrons (groups 1, 2, 13, 14) or 8 minus that number (groups 15–17). Group 2: valence 2 → MO. Group 14: valence 4 → EH₄ (CH₄). Group 16: valence 2 → H₂E (H₂O). Group 15: valence 3 → EH₃ (NH₃). Group 13: valence 3 → E₂O₃ (Al₂O₃).
solution.why_others_wrong: Options containing (c) or (d) are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties', periodic trends in valence

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.question_text: The element with atomic number 114 is placed in the periodic table in:

solution.concept: Predicting the position of a heavy element
solution.explanation: The seventh period begins at Z = 87 and ends at Z = 118 (group 18). Element 114 is four places before 118, so it is in group 18 − 4 = 14, in the p-block of period 7, below lead.
solution.why_others_wrong: Group 16 would be Z = 116. Period 6 ends at Z = 86. Group 4 of period 7 is Z = 104.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties', nomenclature of elements with atomic numbers > 100; long form of periodic table

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The listed atomic radii of the noble gases are larger than those of the halogens of the same periods.
Reason (R): For the noble gases van der Waals (non-bonded) radii are quoted, whereas for the halogens covalent radii are quoted, and van der Waals radii are larger.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.explanation: Noble gases are monatomic and do not form ordinary covalent bonds, so only their van der Waals radii can be measured. A van der Waals radius (half the distance between non-bonded neighbours) is much larger than a covalent radius. This is why the noble gases appear to break the trend of decreasing radius across a period. R explains A.
steps: Noble gases: van der Waals radii
Apparent increase at group 18 is due to the different definition
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties', atomic radius (noble gases)
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Chemical reactivity tends to be high for the elements at the two extremes of a period and lower for the elements in the middle.
Statement II: The high reactivity of the group 1 metals is due to their high ionisation enthalpies.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.explanation: On the left of a period the metals lose electrons readily, and on the right the non-metals gain electrons readily, so reactivity is highest at the two ends: Statement I is true. Alkali metals are reactive because their ionisation enthalpies are low, which makes electron loss easy; Statement II is false.
steps: Left end: easy electron loss (low ΔiH); right end: easy electron gain (very negative ΔegH) (I true)
Group 1 reactivity comes from low, not high, ionisation enthalpy (II false)
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties', periodic trends in chemical properties: reactivity
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Among the hydrides NH₃, PH₃, AsH₃ and SbH₃, the one with the lowest boiling point is:

solution.explanation: From PH₃ to SbH₃ the boiling point rises with molecular size because van der Waals forces increase. NH₃ has an abnormally high boiling point because its molecules are hydrogen bonded. So PH₃ has the lowest boiling point (about 185 K, against about 238 K for NH₃).
steps: PH₃ < AsH₃ < SbH₃: larger molecules, stronger van der Waals forces
NH₃ is raised above PH₃ by hydrogen bonding
solution.why_others_wrong: NH₃ is hydrogen bonded, and AsH₃ and SbH₃ are larger molecules with stronger dispersion forces, so all three boil above PH₃.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'The p-Block Elements', group 15 elements: properties of hydrides

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (group 16 element) with List-II (its nature).

List-I:
A. Oxygen
B. Sulphur
C. Tellurium
D. Polonium

List-II:
I. Metal
II. Metalloid
III. Non-metal, solid at room temperature
IV. Non-metal, gas at room temperature

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: Metallic character increases down group 16: oxygen and sulphur are non-metals (oxygen a gas, sulphur a solid), selenium and tellurium are metalloids and polonium is a metal.
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes interchange oxygen and sulphur, or tellurium and polonium, or sulphur and tellurium.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'The p-Block Elements', group 16 elements: physical properties
solution.final_answer: Option A: A-IV, B-III, C-II, D-I

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Helium has the lowest boiling point of any known substance.
Statement II: The first ionisation enthalpy of the noble gases increases down the group.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Physical properties of the noble gases
solution.explanation: Helium boils at about 4.2 K, the lowest boiling point of any substance, because only very weak dispersion forces act between its tiny atoms: Statement I is true. Down group 18 the atomic size increases, so the ionisation enthalpy decreases: Statement II is false.
steps: He: b.p. ≈ 4.2 K, the lowest known (I true)
Size increases down the group → ΔiH decreases (II false)
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'The p-Block Elements', group 18 elements: physical properties and ionisation enthalpy
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: The first member of each group of the p-block differs from the other members of its group. Which of the following is NOT a reason for this anomalous behaviour?

options.text: Availability of d orbitals in its valence shell

solution.concept: Reasons for the anomalous behaviour of the first member
solution.explanation: The first member of each p-block group is anomalous because of its small size, high electronegativity, high ionisation enthalpy and the ABSENCE of d orbitals in its valence shell (n = 2 has only s and p orbitals).
steps: Second-period valence shell: 2s and 2p only → no d orbitals
Small size, high electronegativity and high ionisation enthalpy are genuine reasons
solution.why_others_wrong: Small size, high electronegativity and high ionisation enthalpy are all listed causes of the anomaly; it is the lack, not the presence, of d orbitals that matters.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'The p-Block Elements', anomalous behaviour of the first member of p-block groups
solution.final_answer: Option D: Availability of d orbitals in its valence shell

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Which element of group 13 has the highest electronegativity (Pauling scale)?

solution.explanation: Boron, the small first member, has the highest electronegativity in the group (about 2.0). Down the group electronegativity first falls from B to Al (1.5) and then rises slightly (Ga 1.6, In 1.7, Tl 1.8) because of differences in atomic size, but none of the heavier members reaches boron's value.
solution.why_others_wrong: The slight rise from Al to Tl misleads some students into choosing Tl or Ga; aluminium has the lowest value in the group.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry (pre-2023 edition), 'The p-Block Elements', group 13 elements: electronegativity

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The heavier elements of groups 15 and 16 can form dπ–pπ bonds, but nitrogen and oxygen cannot.
Reason (R): Nitrogen and oxygen have no d orbitals in their valence shells.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: dπ–pπ bonding and the first element
solution.explanation: Phosphorus and the heavier elements have vacant d orbitals in their valence shells, which they can use to form dπ–pπ bonds (for example with oxygen). Nitrogen and oxygen, in the second period, have only 2s and 2p orbitals, so they cannot form such bonds; they form pπ–pπ multiple bonds instead. R explains A.
steps: Heavier elements: vacant d orbitals → dπ–pπ bonding possible
N, O: no valence d orbitals (R) → no dπ–pπ bonding (A)
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'The p-Block Elements', group 15: anomalous properties of nitrogen
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Down group 15, the covalent radius increases considerably from nitrogen to phosphorus but only slightly from arsenic to bismuth.
Statement II: The small increase from arsenic to bismuth is due to the presence of completely filled d and/or f orbitals in the heavier members, which shield the nucleus poorly.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.explanation: Both statements describe the NCERT trend. A new shell causes a large jump from N to P. In As, Sb and Bi the extra nuclear charge is poorly shielded by filled d (and in Bi also f) orbitals, so the radius increases only slightly.
steps: As → Bi: small increase due to poor shielding by d/f electrons (II true)
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'The p-Block Elements', group 15 elements: atomic and ionic radii
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (group) with List-II (trend in oxidation state down the group, due to the inert pair effect).

List-I:
A. Group 13
B. Group 14
C. Group 15
D. Group 16

List-II:
I. +3 becomes more stable than +5
II. +1 becomes more stable than +3
III. +4 becomes more stable than +6
IV. +2 becomes more stable than +4

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: Down groups 13 to 16 the ns² electrons become increasingly reluctant to take part in bonding, so an oxidation state two less than the group oxidation state becomes more stable for the heavier members.
steps: Group 13 (ns² np¹): +1 more stable than +3 down the group (e.g. Tl) → II
Group 14 (ns² np²): +2 more stable than +4 (e.g. Pb) → IV
Group 15 (ns² np³): +3 more stable than +5 (e.g. Bi) → I
Group 16 (ns² np⁴): +4 more stable than +6 → III
solution.why_others_wrong: Each group's lower stable state is the group oxidation state minus two; the other codes break this pattern.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'The p-Block Elements', oxidation states of groups 15 and 16; Class 11 Chemistry (pre-2023 edition), 'The p-Block Elements', groups 13 and 14
solution.final_answer: Option B: A-II, B-IV, C-I, D-III

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about the group 17 elements are correct?

(a) They have the smallest atomic radii in their respective periods.
(b) The bond dissociation enthalpy of I₂ is higher than that of Br₂.
(c) They have very high ionisation enthalpies, so they have little tendency to lose electrons.
(d) Their melting and boiling points increase steadily from fluorine to iodine.
(e) Iodine is more electronegative than chlorine.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: Halogens have the highest effective nuclear charge in their periods, hence the smallest radii and very high ionisation enthalpies. Their melting and boiling points rise with molecular size from F₂ to I₂. The bond dissociation enthalpy decreases from Cl₂ to I₂ (Cl₂ > Br₂ > I₂) as the atoms get larger, and electronegativity decreases down the group.
solution.why_others_wrong: Options containing (b) or (e) are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'The p-Block Elements', group 17 elements: atomic and physical properties

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Which of the following correctly describes the tendency of the group 14 elements to show catenation?

options.text: All five elements catenate strongly, in the order C > Si > Ge > Sn > Pb
Sn > Ge > Si > C; lead catenates the most
C ≫ Si > Ge ≈ Sn; lead does not show catenation

solution.explanation: Catenation depends on the strength of the E–E bond. The C–C bond is strong, so carbon catenates far more than any other element. E–E bond strength falls down the group, giving C ≫ Si > Ge ≈ Sn, and lead does not show catenation.
solution.why_others_wrong: Silicon catenates much less than carbon. Lead does not catenate, so orders that include strong catenation by Pb, or that reverse the trend, are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry (pre-2023 edition), 'The p-Block Elements', group 14 elements: anomalous behaviour of carbon (catenation)
solution.final_answer: Option D: C ≫ Si > Ge ≈ Sn; lead does not show catenation

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The tendency of the group 15 elements to show the −3 oxidation state decreases down the group.
Reason (R): The electronegativity of the elements increases down group 15.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.explanation: Down group 15 the atoms get larger and more metallic, so the tendency to gain three electrons (−3 state) decreases; bismuth hardly forms any compound in the −3 state. A is true. Electronegativity decreases, not increases, down the group, so R is false.
steps: Size and metallic character increase down the group → −3 tendency decreases (A true)
Electronegativity: N > P > As > Sb > Bi (R false)
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'The p-Block Elements', group 15 elements: oxidation states
solution.final_answer: Option C: A is true but R is false.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: The colour of the halogens becomes lighter from F₂ to I₂.
Statement II: The halogens are coloured because their molecules absorb radiation in the visible region, which excites their outer electrons to higher energy levels.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.explanation: The halogens are coloured because absorption of visible light excites their outer electrons; the colour seen is the complementary colour. As the molecules get larger, less energy is needed for the excitation, so the colour deepens from pale yellow F₂ to violet I₂. Statement I is false; Statement II is true.
steps: Absorption of visible light → electronic excitation → colour (II true)
Smaller excitation energy down the group → colour deepens, not lightens (I false)
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'The p-Block Elements', group 17 elements: physical properties
solution.final_answer: Option D: Statement I is false but Statement II is true.
